content_items.title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) for RASD: The Flemish Biodiversity Portal Approach

programme.title: [No sound] Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) for RASD: The Flemish Biodiversity Portal Approach
programme.session: SYM23 To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
programme.abstract:
Managing Restricted Access Species Data (RASD) becomes complex when regional portals must balance local sensitivity requirements with global data sharing through aggregators like GBIF. The Flemish Biodiversity Portal (VBP), built on the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA), addresses this by utilizing a "twin dataset" architecture, ensuring that high-resolution data remains secure while a more generalized version is made publicly available. This strategy prevents the exposure of precise coordinates on global platforms while the dataset structure, metadata and most of the identifiers stay the same.

In this presentation, we detail how VBP manages these twins using Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) logic embedded within the dynamicProperties field. By utilizing machine-readable flags-such as {"rbac":true, "rbac_allowed":"HIGHRES"}-the portal dynamically determines data visibility. Users with authorized roles access the high-resolution "twin," while the general public is directed to the low-resolution version.

This dual-dataset approach ensures that "not seeing" high-resolution data is a deliberate, governed choice rather than a technical limitation. We will discuss the synchronization challenges inherent in maintaining twins and how this workflow aligns with the TDWG RASD extension’s goal of standardizing the reasons and treatments for data restriction. By providing a transparent metadata trail for why a dataset is restricted or generalized, VBP demonstrates a scalable model for regional nodes to contribute to the global biodiversity data commons without compromising local conservation priorities.

content_items.title: Restricted access species data in Finland

programme.title: [No sound] Restricted access species data in Finland
programme.session: SYM23 To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
programme.abstract: The Finnish Act on the Openness of Government Activities (621/1999) necessitates that species data in Finland is not made publicly available if it would endanger the protection of the species or area in question. The Finnish Biodiversity Information Facility (FinBIF) is a service for researchers, government and the public. The data harmonised in FinBIF's data warehouse includes the results of national monitoring programs, scientific collections and citizen science projects. FinBIF is the body primarily responsible for managing Finnish restricted access species data (RASD). FinBIF coordinates an expert panel, the Public Authorities Working Group, that maintains a list of taxa that require some level of data restriction. The Public Authorities Working Group determines the level of restriction and circumstances under which it should be applied. Each taxon included on the list must be subject to a concrete threat: persecution, harvesting, or disturbance. The list was first compiled in 2015, and a comprehensive update was carried out in 2025. Minor updates are made as needed. There are currently 155 listed taxa. Species data that is mobilised by FinBIF has restrictions applied on being harmonised in the data warehouse, before being made publicly available. The unrestricted data is made available in a parallel data warehouse that can only be accessed by registered users from statutory public authorities. Other data users may make a request for access to restricted data. Requests are fulfilled via a data access platform on a case by case basis with the consent of the data providers or relevant proxies. We outline the system for handling RASD in Finland and discuss how current and proposed biodiversity data standards may aid data providers and users.

actual.identification_notes: The beginning of the talk (and its introduction) is lost in the no-sound period; the recording picks up mid-talk at 00:17:29. Identified from the Finnish content, FinBIF references and the convener addressing 'Will' at 00:24:04; Will Morris also answers in later Q&A as the FinBIF speaker.

content_items.summary: The recorded portion of Will Morris' talk explains how FinBIF applies Finland's government-maintained restricted species list (first published 2015, updated 2025, a little over 150 species) to all data it mediates. Restrictions range from full concealment to generalisation to 1-100 km grids and may be limited by region, season or specific sites; field notes are withheld and multi-record events are unlinked so co-observed species cannot reveal locations. Restricted data are published through a public portal and API, while a logged government authorities portal gives unrestricted access and a request service lets others ask providers for restricted data. He noted that GBIF-bound Darwin Core Archives only use informationWithheld and dataGeneralizations, and that much of the restriction information has no standard home yet.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: FinBIF applies an authority-maintained restricted species list to all mediated data, but lacks a standard way to share what it restricted and why.
content_items.why_it_matters: A national-scale implementation showing both the mechanics of restricting data (generalisation, unlinking events) and the gap that motivates the TDWG RASD extension.
key_points: A working group of government authorities (e.g. Finnish Environment Institute, Parks and Wildlife) maintains the list of restricted species and the restrictions to apply; the list was first published in 2015 and updated in 2025.
FinBIF conservatively applies these restrictions to all data it mediates, not only government data.

The list has just over 150 species and mirrors taxonomic bias: about half are birds (about a third of Finland's breeding birds), nearly all bats, some reptiles, amphibians, butterflies and a moth, and many vascular plants (largely orchids).
Restrictions include full concealment or generalisation to 1, 5, 10, 25, 50 or 100 km grids, possibly limited to parts of Finland, seasons (breeding, wintering) or specific sites.
Field notes that might reveal locations are withheld, and multi-record events are unlinked so an unrestricted co-observed species does not reveal a restricted one.

A public portal, API and bulk download service (with persistent identifiers) serve restricted data; a separate logged authorities portal gives unrestricted access to government employees; others can use a data request service mediated between users and providers.

Data published to GBIF use Darwin Core informationWithheld and dataGeneralizations, but the sensitive species checklist is only an Excel spreadsheet and information about restricting entities and access routes is not shared via any standard.

notable_claims.claim: Finland's restricted species list has a little over 150 species, about half of them birds.
FinBIF applies the restrictions to all data it mediates, not just government-sourced data.
Much of FinBIF's information on restrictions is not shared via any data standard; the rarity checklist is only an Excel spreadsheet.

results_findings: Records from multi-record events are unlinked to avoid inferring restricted locations from co-observed species.
limitations: Information on who applies restrictions, where unrestricted data can be obtained and what exactly has been withheld cannot currently be shared in a standard way.
future_work: Share restriction information via Darwin Core Archives or Data Packages once the TDWG task group's extension exists.

notable_moments.description: Overview of the kinds of restrictions applied (concealment, grids, region, season, site).
Unlinking multi-record events to protect restricted species.
Gap: restriction information not shareable in any standard.

content_items.title: Restricted Access Species Data: The Swedish Model

programme.title: Restricted Access Species Data: The Swedish Model
programme.session: SYM23 To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
programme.abstract:
For some 20 years, Sweden has used a central system, UserAdmin, for managing users and their roles. Certain roles decide which restricted access species data (RASD) a user is authorized to view. Out of the more than 158 million records in the Species Observation System (SOS) about 1.5 million are protected, belonging to 111 different species.

Records are automatically obscured if a species belongs to any of classes 3-5 on the national protection list. Additionally, a reporter can choose to manually hide any of their observations up until a future date of their choice. These will be handled as if they belong to class 3.

A protected observation is still visible to the reporter and the observers. They can also be available to authorized verifiers, authorities and agencies.

How can RASD be utilized?

1) A user can ask authorized staff in the local region if there is anything of concern in a certain area. They can give advice without revealing any sensitive data.

2) Upon authorization, some authorities/agencies can use Signal Search that answers yes/no if anything can be found that matches a broader taxonomic and geographic selection.

3) Restricted access can only be granted a person, who will then be screened in accordance with Swedish law and must sign a non-disclosure contract. This person is either allowed to do their own searches or to receive specific exports made by authorized staff. Receiving such exports is free of charge for official authorities but comes with a fee for commercial requests.

All observations in SOS can be accessed by logging in to either the web application Fynddata (fynddata.artdatabanken.se), maintained by SLU Swedish Species Information Centre, or Artsök (www.artkoll.se/artsok), a GIS based system managed by the County Administrative Board.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Johan Wiljegard' (ASR) from the Swedish Species Information Centre; content matches the abstract (UserAdmin, SOS, 158 million/1.5 million records).

content_items.summary: Johan Liljeblad traced Sweden's handling of restricted species data from a simple role table in the first citizen-science observatory (2000) to the UserAdmin role system launched with Artportalen 2 (2014) and a federation system harvesting other datasets (2021). About 1.5 million of 158 million records, belonging to 111 species, are protected in diffusion classes (5, 25 or 50 km squares), with users also able to hide or diffuse their own records. He explained authorised access via contracts, three access systems and 'signal search', which tells authorised users whether any sensitive records exist in an area without revealing species, and noted the trend is to restrict less over time.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Sweden combines a long-running role system, diffusion classes and a yes/no 'signal search' to manage 1.5 million protected records while gradually restricting fewer species.
content_items.why_it_matters: Illustrates a mature national approach with practical tools (signal search, logged searches, delegated role management) and identifies the need for standardised authorised APIs and verification categories to exchange sensitive data.
key_points: Timeline: 2000 citizen observatory with one role per account; offline sensitive observation database until 2008; 2014 UserAdmin with Artportalen 2 allowing role switching; 2021 federation system harvesting other Swedish datasets via APIs; new version of UserAdmin a few years ago.
About 158 million records in total, of which about 1.5 million are protected, belonging to 111 species; the list is published as an Excel spreadsheet.
Protection classes generalise to 5, 25 or 50 km squares; users can hide their own observation until a future date (treated as class three) or privately diffuse it.
The system is revised roughly every five years, and the trend is to restrict less, because hidden observations can't be protected if nobody knows about them.

Access routes: ask authorised staff, signal search, or sign a contract giving access to certain classes, usually for a region and taxonomic group; accessed through Artsök, Navet (Swedish Forest Agency) and the Centre's own system.

County administrative boards grant roles to their own staff, so role management is not centralised; searches are logged so leaks can be traced, though leaks usually come from Facebook groups or research papers.

Signal search answers yes/no for whether sensitive data exist in an area for a list of species, with at least a one-year date window; large diffusion areas (e.g. nesting eagles) make it say yes for much of southern Sweden.
Harvesting sensitive data from iNaturalist and observation.org needs authorised APIs and standardised verification categories so verified records can be returned to source.

notable_claims.claim: About 1.5 million of about 158 million Swedish records, belonging to 111 species, are protected.
The trend in Sweden is to restrict fewer species over time because hidden observations are hard to protect.
Leaks usually come from Facebook groups or research papers rather than the system.

recommendations: Standardise authorised APIs for exchanging sensitive data and the verification categories used when returning verified records to source datasets.
limitations: Signal search says yes too often for widely diffused species such as nesting eagles.
No authorised APIs yet for harvesting sensitive data from other platforms.

notable_moments.description: Scale: 1.5 million protected records out of 158 million.
How signal search works.
Need for standards for harvesting sensitive data and returning verifications.

content_items.title: Toward RASD Implementation in Brazil: Integrating Conservation, Open Data, and Traditional Knowledge Safeguards

programme.title: Toward RASD Implementation in Brazil: Integrating Conservation, Open Data, and Traditional Knowledge Safeguards
programme.session: SYM23 To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
programme.abstract: Brazil, a megadiverse country with extraordinary biological and sociocultural diversity, faces complex challenges in managing and publishing Restricted Access Species Data (RASD). Open-access platforms strengthen science, conservation, and policy, but also amplify risks of misuse of sensitive information. Sensitivity varies across taxonomic groups and use contexts. Key concerns include illegal hunting, wildlife trafficking, predatory collection of commercially valuable species, and pressure on threatened, endemic, or low-density populations. A further dimension involves species linked to associated traditional knowledge (ATK) of Indigenous peoples and local communities. Frameworks such as the CBD, Nagoya Protocol, ILO Convention 169, and Brazil's Law 13.123/2015 require free, prior, and informed consent for use of these resources-rarely met in practice. They provide important safeguards but also reveal limits: fragmented implementation, weak traceability, and uneven recognition of community protocols. Paradoxically, traditional territories remain a critical gap in national repositories, despite their recognized role in conservation. Precise occurrence data are essential for monitoring, enforcement, and policy, producing tension between FAIR and CARE principles and effective protection. We discuss challenges faced by Brazilian data providers in handling RASD and present approaches for differentiated access, including spatial generalization, multi-level sensitivity classification, and controlled access to precise coordinates. The work aligns with TDWG efforts on vocabularies and metadata extensions for RASD, advancing interoperable solutions that balance transparency, conservation, ATK protection, and visibility of traditional communities in biodiversity science.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as Clara Baringo from the 'Brazilian Biodiversity Information System'; content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Clara Baringo Fonseca explained that Brazil's national biodiversity information system currently handles sensitive data only by generalisation, informationWithheld and splitting data into private and public datasets. She identified three areas needing distinct rules: endangered species, ongoing research, and socio-biodiversity data and traditional knowledge. Focusing on the last, she argued that communities must control their data, that it is often attributes such as uses, local names or preparation methods rather than the species that must be restricted, and that semi-restricted access (for example for the patent office) and traceability are needed.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Protecting traditional knowledge requires community-controlled, attribute-level and semi-restricted access, not just hiding species locations.
content_items.why_it_matters: Brings Indigenous and traditional knowledge into the RASD discussion and shows that restriction needs go beyond location obfuscation of threatened species.
key_points: Brazil's system is growing fast and is trying to repatriate Brazilian data held in repositories outside the country.
Currently only dataGeneralizations, informationWithheld and separate private/public datasets are used.

Three topic areas with different risks and access rules: endangered species (hunting, trafficking), ongoing research, and socio-biodiversity data/traditional knowledge (misappropriation via biopiracy).
International law is not enough; systems must carry community-defined conditions at data level and within a legal framework.
Traditional territories are underrepresented in repositories, but without restriction mechanisms there is little point collecting more data; FAIR and CARE principles should both apply.

Needs include appropriate public metadata, community authorisation of what is shared, semi-restricted access (e.g. patent office can check whether a species has associated traditional knowledge) and traceability.
Use cases: religious or sacred use (kept only for preservation), species use (attributes restricted), and hunting inside protected areas that managers want to monitor.
Restrictable attributes include scientific or local names, type of use, preparation method, time and location; control must always rest with the community.

notable_claims.claim: For traditional knowledge it is usually not the species but its attributes (use, local name, preparation) that must be restricted.
Without mechanisms to restrict data there is little point adding more data from traditional territories.

recommendations: Give communities control over what is sensitive and who can access it.
Provide semi-restricted access, e.g. for patent offices, and traceability of data use.
examples_case_studies: Sacred/religious use knowledge kept only for community preservation.
Monitoring sustainable hunting by communities within protected areas.

notable_moments.description: Three categories needing different access rules.
Three traditional-knowledge use cases.
It is the attributes, not the species, that need restricting.

content_items.title: The Edge: Insights into problems that arise from implementing data solutions for restricted access (sensitive) species data

programme.title: The Edge: Insights into problems that arise from implementing data solutions for restricted access (sensitive) species data
programme.session: SYM23 To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
programme.abstract: With the rising of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, organisations and individuals are increasingly concerned about data on species that they wish to restrict for a wide variety of reasons including everything from the terms and conditions of data licence agreements through to concern about the poaching of attractive species. These so-called sensitive species or restricted access species data (RASD), present problems for the public display, dissemination and use of biodiversity data. Common treatment approaches to RASD involve generalising data through truncation of latitude and longitude, using grids to display data, or withholding points altogether. Many implementations use a list of identified sensitive species as the basis of generalisation. The Atlas of Living Australia (ALA) is a collaborative, digital, open infrastructure displaying biodiversity data from multiple sources, making it accessible and reusable. Data is presented in a consistent, current form, taking into account RASD, for scientists, policy makers, environmental planners, land managers, and industry. To do this, the ALA complies with 8 different approaches to RASD across governments jurisdictions as well as the requirements of diverse entities, from iNaturalist to Indigenous communities. Australia developed an agreed national framework for the management and sharing of RASD in 2023 (www.rasd.ord.au). In developing governance mechanisms to implement the framework, we have identified a range of surprising issues surrounding RASD arising from the complexities of taxonomy, geography and data coming from different sources with different approaches. We will discuss these issues and what responses the ALA has developed to each of them in order to represent data as systematically as possible.

actual.identification_notes: Presented by the session convener himself ('I'm the next speaker'); title referenced as 'The Edge' from U2.

content_items.summary: Convener Cameron Slatyer presented the Atlas of Living Australia's experience of edge cases that arise when implementing RASD treatments across more than 184 million records using government-supplied lists. Taxonomy was the biggest problem: undescribed species, disagreements between states, and mismatch between subspecies-level sensitivity and species-level data force precautionary generalisation at higher ranks or whole species. Data errors (wrong coordinates outside a treatment polygon, names or locality in the wrong field, as common with eDNA data) can expose restricted data, and AI mining makes such leaks easier, including an experimental ALA AI tool that exposed a locality recorded in the wrong field.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Plan RASD treatments carefully, because taxonomy, data errors and associated records can silently defeat simple rules like 'generalise to 10 km'.
content_items.why_it_matters: Practical lessons from one of the largest RASD implementations, directly relevant to anyone automating sensitive-data treatments.
key_points: Reasons for RASD range from conservation to discouraging entry to bombing ranges and protecting biosecurity eradication sites for trade reasons.

The ALA applies treatments (withholding records and images, generalising, modifying fields) to over 184 million records, driven by lists from state, territory and Commonwealth governments, plus data-provider requests.
Main message: plan the approach - what is being restricted, flow-on effects, and risks.
Taxonomic problems: undescribed RASD species, disagreement among states over current names, and sensitivity at subspecies level while providers supply species-level data (or vice versa).

Rule of thumb: when taxonomic resolution can't be resolved, go up a level; species absent from the backbone attach at genus, so genus-level records get generalised; populations can't be delineated, so the whole species is generalised.
Data errors can expose RASD: erroneous coordinates outside a treatment polygon, scientific names in the wrong field (common in eDNA data with BIN numbers), and locality in the wrong field.
AI makes such errors easier to mine; an experimental ALA AI tool mining iNaturalist data exposed a sensitive species because locality was in the wrong field.

notable_claims.claim: The ALA applies obfuscations to over 184 million records.
Taxonomy is an absolute nightmare when implementing RASD based on species lists.
Erroneous coordinates outside a treatment polygon can leave RASD fully exposed.
AI makes it easy to mine and return information that was thought hidden or altered.

recommendations: Plan your approach: consider what is being restricted, the flow-on effects and the risks of each treatment.
limitations: Precautionary generalisation at higher ranks generalises many unnecessary records.
examples_case_studies: Subspecies flagged sensitive while the provider only supplies species-level data.
eDNA datasets with BIN numbers in the name field.
Experimental AI mining iNaturalist data exposing a misplaced locality.

representative_excerpt.text: So our principal take-home message that underpins all of these issues that we're going to raise is basically making sure you plan your approach.

notable_moments.description: Taxonomy as the biggest RASD implementation problem.
Three common taxonomic edge cases and how the ALA handles them.
Data errors and AI mining exposing restricted data.

content_items.title: Using wildlife trade data to support proactive RASD decision-making

programme.title: Using wildlife trade data to support proactive RASD decision-making
programme.session: SYM23 To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
programme.abstract: The poaching of wildlife is a growing biodiversity threat, with online trade increasingly facilitating exploitation. Wildlife traders monitor publications, biodiversity repositories, and social media to identify desirable species, and trade activity reveals species being poached prior to formal conservation assessment. While biodiversity data are fundamental to conservation and research it can also increase exploitation of vulnerable taxa. A challenge for RASD frameworks is the time lag between species discovery, conservation assessment, and data restriction. During this period, biodiversity databases may expose species to collection pressure before threats are formally recognised. Current approaches to sensitive species data management are often reactive, relying on formal conservation status or legal protection. This issue is particularly relevant for terrestrial invertebrates, many of which are newly described, range-restricted, data deficient, and increasingly targeted in wildlife trade. Public occurrence datasets are often the only available locality information for these taxa. In Australia, the recent restriction of occurrence data for the trapdoor spider Moggridgea rainbowi following a suspected poaching incident demonstrates adaptive data governance and underscores the value of extending precautionary approaches to additional vulnerable wildlife taxa. We propose that wildlife trade data can function as an early-warning indicator for identifying species subject to poaching and exploitation, and for determining when occurrence data warrant precautionary restriction, prior to formal conservation assessment. Incorporating wildlife trade data into RASD frameworks supports proactive biodiversity data governance and can reduce exploitation risk from data accessibility.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by the convener after slide problems; content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: PhD researcher Charlotte Lassaline argued that RASD lists, which rely on formal conservation assessments, are biased towards well-studied vertebrates and miss poorly known, range-restricted invertebrates that are increasingly sought in wildlife trade. Using the Kangaroo Island pygmy trapdoor spider, whose public data were restricted within about two weeks of a reported poaching incident, she contrasted reactive and proactive approaches. She proposed a wildlife trade species sensitivity framework combining trade-demand measures with weighted biological sensitivity factors into a vulnerability index to flag species for data protection before formal assessment.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Wildlife trade data can act as an early warning system to protect species' locality data before formal conservation assessments catch up.
content_items.why_it_matters: Offers a practical, evidence-based way to prioritise species for data restriction, particularly for invertebrates that formal lists overlook.
key_points: Wildlife trade is predicted to affect one in five species worldwide; poachers use public occurrence data to locate species.
RASD lists are largely informed by formal assessments (IUCN Red List, CITES, government lists) that are slow and data-hungry.
Only about 1.4% of insects and just over 1% of arachnids have been evaluated by the IUCN Red List, versus most vertebrates.
Invertebrates are often newly described, range-restricted and data deficient, yet increasingly desired by collectors; public occurrence data may be the only information on where they occur.
There is a 'window of vulnerability' between exploitation starting and formal recognition and legal protection.
Kangaroo Island pygmy trapdoor spider: nationally endangered after bushfires but data still public; a poaching incident reported to the ALA led to restriction within about two weeks (reactive).

Proposed framework: trade demand (number of adverts, individuals traded, market value) plus weighted biological sensitivity factors (distribution, population size, reproductive output, dispersal) produce a vulnerability index.
High-index species already protected should be considered for RASD listing; unassessed ones are candidates for investigation; data should be obscured not removed, available on request, and reviewed.
methods: vulnerability index from weighted sensitivity factors

notable_claims.claim: Wildlife trade is predicted to affect one in every five species worldwide.
Only 1.4% of insects and just over 1% of arachnids have had their conservation status evaluated by the IUCN.
After a reported poaching incident, the spider's data were restricted online in less than about two weeks.

recommendations: Use trade pressure as an early indicator of exploitation risk for RASD decisions.
Obscure rather than remove sensitive locality data, keep access by request, and review restrictions as research emerges.
examples_case_studies: Kangaroo Island pygmy trapdoor spider poaching incident.

representative_excerpt.text: So importantly, this means the trade pressure can be considered as an early indicator of exploitation risk. It doesn't necessarily tell us that a species is vulnerable, but it tells us that a species is being exposed to a pressure that may lead to it being threatened in the very near future.

notable_moments.description: IUCN Red List coverage gap for insects and arachnids.
Kangaroo Island pygmy trapdoor spider case.
The wildlife trade species sensitivity framework.

content_items.title: A new standard for restricted access (sensitive) species data

programme.title: A new standard for restricted access (sensitive) species data
programme.session: SYM23 To see or not to see - that is the question. Managing restricted access data (RASD)
programme.abstract: There is growing concern among many organisations and researchers about so-called sensitive species or restricted access species data (RASD), that is, data that needs to be modified or withheld from the general public. This data is intrinsically difficult to share or display and the existing Darwin Core fields no longer give data managers the flexibility to deal with the diverse array of emerging issues that managers encounter. Following a workshop in 2023, a Darwin Core Task Group was established on sensitive species data. The Task Group has developed a suite of reasons and treatments and an underlying vocabulary that enables data managers to communicate what has happened to restricted data and why in line with FAIR principles. The data extension is intended to handle a wide range of reasons for restricted access and a similarly wide range of treatment options that can be applied to the data. This proposed data extension paths the way for institutions, regions or countries to develop a consistent approach to the management of restricted data. We will outline and discuss the new restricted access species data extension, including solutions for both Darwin Core Native and Darwin Core Data Packages.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Tanya Latey' (ASR) from the ALA; content matches the abstract.

She showed how treatments attach to records in Darwin Core Archives (as a star-schema extension) and Darwin Core Data Package (via join tables), walked through the treatment fields, and demonstrated a cave case study with a troglobitic spider, fossils and undescribed mites.

content_items.summary: Two panel Q&A sessions chaired by Cameron Slatyer: an impromptu one on the first four talks when the session ran ahead of schedule, and a longer one with all speakers after the final talk. Topics included the real cost of managing sensitivities (several FTE in Sweden, monthly list updates at the ALA, opportunity cost), breaches (none known), personal privacy of collectors, whether generative AI already exposes locations, obfuscation on request of data collectors (e.g. pest hunting and Indigenous datasets), taxonomic upscaling, names that reveal localities, correlated fields such as collector and date, historical data, informationWithheld usage, and the feasibility for global collections like the Smithsonian. key_points: Cost: Sweden has about three FTE handling access contracts; FinBIF sees a large hidden human cost and opportunity cost; the ALA updates RASD lists monthly but estimates about a million records came in only because RASD treatment was available.
No panellist knew of data breaches; Will Morris argued habitat loss, not knowledge of locations, is the main threat and 'security by obscurity' is a poor conservation tool.
Collector privacy (Kew question): Sweden requires contactable reporters but allows hiding observations; INBO sometimes attributes data to a team rather than individuals.
Generative AI (Gemini, ChatGPT) could already reveal where the Kangaroo Island spider lives because the data were mined years ago, though a long-restricted species was refused.

content_items.title: Open Digital Curation Needs: openness, interoperability, provenance

programme.title: Open Digital Curation Needs: openness, interoperability, provenance
programme.session: SYM13A Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Moving toward open digital curation to make round-tripping possible, consider the necessary interplay of three facets: openness, interoperability, and provenance. Via open application programming interfaces (APIs), data becomes accessible to humans and AI. Given openness, interoperability becomes possible and offers opportunities to contribute and collaborate. We share three examples here: [iNaturalist (iNat)](https://www.inaturalist.org/), the [Catalogue of Life (COL)](https://www.catalogueoflife.org/), and the [Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF](https://www.gbif.org/)). With iNat's open APIs, our researchers using [TaxonWorks (TW)](https://taxonworks.org/) can pull images and related data into TW. In the other direction, iNat curators submit or point their users to the specific gitHub repository to log taxonomic inquiries directly to those curating these data. This reduces steps (e. g. emails) needed to get to round-tripping. From TW, our collections data go straight to GBIF. We grab the GBIF-related ingestion feedback directly into TW to again reduce the human mental data curation burden and imagine future automated validation. Our taxonomic data flow interoperably between TW to COL via [Checklist Bank](https://www.checklistbank.org/). To do all of the above, we must decide on and use identifiers (e. g. [ORCiD](https://orcid.org/)s, [Wikidata Q numbers] (https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q43649390)) and the related metadata that helps us ensure we have a provenance trail. Understanding our data through these breadcrumbs provides the foundation for round-tripping. In TW, imagine extracting data from literature using large language models (LLMs). Our communities need software and APIs to vet the resulting data, along with robust provenance. We find it's these decisions, usually human-mediated, that are difficult to capture in context, for example, with the user interface. When we connect via our APIs for data exchange, what must we persist? What can be temporary?

content_items.summary: Deborah (Debbie) Paul, from the team behind TaxonWorks, Catalogue of Life work and Global Names, argued that open digital curation - built on openness, interoperability, provenance and identifiers - empowers wider participation and shortens the path from spotting an error to fixing it. Examples included Bionomia profiles that keep deceased collectors' expertise attributed, an iNaturalist user fixing names directly in the Orthoptera Species File, and TaxonWorks features letting projects search and clone each other's controlled vocabularies linked to ontologies. She welcomed agents (including LLMs) with roles in the Darwin Core Data Package, raised questions about what provenance we must now track for AI use, and asked how shifting openness (API keys, CC0 to CC BY, logins) will affect interoperability.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Open digital curation increases transparency, agency and trust and reduces latency, but needs new provenance practices for AI.

content_items.title: Machine-Ready Botanical Data: Mapping Integrated Collections and Traits with Darwin Core Data Package

programme.title: Machine-Ready Botanical Data: Mapping Integrated Collections and Traits with Darwin Core Data Package
programme.session: SYM13A Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
The Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) provides a powerful foundation for representing biodiversity data in ways that are both AI-ready and round-trip capable. We present a DwC-DP concept mapping developed for the Missouri Botanical Garden (MBG) that integrates herbarium specimens, living collections, and trait (extended specimen) data within a unified framework. To our knowledge, this represents the first detailed cross-collection DwC-DP concept map in the botanical domain, demonstrating how heterogeneous institutional data can be aligned into a coherent, machine-actionable structure.

We identify key areas in the mapping where controlled vocabularies are needed to further define the standard within the relevant communities. In particular, traits and character states constitute a critical class of information for AI applications, such as taxon identification and ecological modeling. While DwC-DP provides a structural basis for integrating such data, practical use requires alignment with external ontologies. We discuss an approach under development at MBG to integrate a trait ontology with DwC-DP, building on an internal pilot system.

Furthermore, we examine a gap in the current design relevant to AI-readiness around identifications: the need to capture not only the data that informs a determination, but the evidentiary and procedural basis for the decision. We consider how such information might be modeled externally to the core design.

This work highlights both the immediate utility of DwC-DP for institutional integration and the collaborative work needed, particularly around shared vocabularies, to advance interoperable and AI-ready botanical data systems.

content_items.summary: Nathan VanderKraats presented a draft mapping of Missouri Botanical Garden's collections to the Darwin Core Data Package, used as an integration layer across independently developed living collections, herbarium and trait data. He highlighted the value of a semantic graph (queries that work whether or not a system has Tropicos' intermediate 'collection' level) and walked through living collections, herbarium identifications and a detailed specimen traits section distinguishing material assertions, media, regions of interest, traits and ML features with human and AI agents. He argued that capturing which traits drove an identification is a separate problem outside the data package, and invited community input to turn the draft into a botanical profile.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Darwin Core Data Package can serve as a semantic integration layer for a botanical garden's diverse collections and trait data, and MBG's draft mapping is offered for community refinement.
content_items.why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, institution-scale application of the newly ratified Darwin Core Data Package, including AI-relevant trait and media modelling.

Boxes show both the official DwC-DP class and a convenience label (e.g. 'specimen' for Material).
Tropicos has an extra 'collection' layer (duplicates from one plant/population) between collection event and specimen; graph queries can answer 'how many specimens from this event?' regardless.
DwC-DP as an integration layer across independently developed databases, with a warehouse-like relational layer on top; knowledge graphs can improve LLM querying of large databases.
Some constraints must be enforced externally, e.g. accession numbers shared between organism and seed material, and only one accepted identification per occurrence.
Identifications link to materials and media (specimen, DNA sequence, photograph) as evidence.

Traits section: material assertions by humans on physical specimens; media file vs media content; regions of interest and transformations; traits vs ML features; human and AI agents; hyperspectral classes (see Matt Austin's talk).
Controlled vocabularies and identifiers for fields are the next area needing community alignment.

Capturing which traits informed an identification is external to what the data package should capture.

content_items.title: From Images to Structured Data: A Scalable AI Workflow for Natural History Museums

programme.title: From Images to Structured Data: A Scalable AI Workflow for Natural History Museums
programme.session: SYM13A Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Natural history museums worldwide face a major digitisation backlog. To unlock this critical bottleneck in research, the biodiversity informatics community is rapidly developing AI-based workflows to automate specimen label transcription and thus speed up the digitisation process. We present here a case study in which we describe an effective AI workflow for extracting specimen label data using Gemini 3.

The workflow combines batch processing with a two-stage Gemini large language model pipeline via API integrations. High-resolution specimen images are first processed to transcribe handwritten and printed labels. After post-processing to remove duplicate data, extract identifiers and fix common transcription errors, the cleaned transcriptions are resubmitted for data structuring using a predefined JSON schema aligned with collection management requirements.

A central design principle is provenance-aware, non-destructive integration of the data into the Finnish museum collection management system. Existing human-curated data are never overwritten. The workflow also records metadata describing which fields were generated by AI, while process-level provenance metadata are archived to support transparency, auditability, and reproducibility.

To support scalable quality assurance, the pipeline automatically generates validation reports from a random sample for human review. Our presentation discusses workflow architecture, provenance strategies, validation models, and lessons learned from deploying AI-assisted transcription at an institutional scale.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Anna Koivunen' (ASR).

content_items.summary: Anne Koivunen, head of digitisation at Luomus, described a pragmatic AI pipeline for tackling a backlog of 10 million undigitised specimens with fewer staff and a goal of full digitisation by 2045. Label images go to Gemini 2.5 for verbatim transcription, then again with a prompt and schema for structured data saved into the Kotka collection management system; for messy vascular plant and moss labels an 'intent' step asks the model what the writer meant. AI output never overrides human-transcribed fields, is flagged, and run metadata (model version, prompts) is stored. She stressed that winning collection staff's trust was harder than the AI itself.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A simple 'just do it' AI transcription pipeline with schema prompts, an intent step and full provenance can make label digitisation scale.
content_items.why_it_matters: A realistic, production-oriented example from a mid-sized museum showing both technical choices and the organisational change needed to adopt AI transcription.

Strategy goal: digitise everything by 2045, requiring about 30% faster digitisation despite staff cuts.
Scalability means variety as well as volume: taxon-specific label types, handwritten/typed, multilingual (Finnish, Swedish, Russian), corrections and differing collection traditions.

Pipeline: images -> Gemini 2.5 verbatim transcription (1-5 hours per batch) -> post-processing -> Gemini with prompt and schema for structuring -> Kotka CMS; the schema is the most important part of the prompt.
Complex labels get an extra 'intent' step interpreting what the writer meant, giving near-correct output even for heavily corrected labels.

Verbatim text is stored in a dedicated field; structured data goes to specific fields, flagged as AI-generated, never overriding human transcription; model versions and prompts are stored.
Case study of 30,000 specimens with 600 (2%) reviewed; future review may drop to 1% focused on difficult labels.

content_items.title: Closing the Loop: The DiSSCo Annotation Validation Framework for Trustworthy Data Round-Tripping

programme.title: Closing the Loop: The DiSSCo Annotation Validation Framework for Trustworthy Data Round-Tripping
programme.session: SYM13A Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
The Distributed System of Scientific Collections (DiSSCo) represents a paradigm shift in specimen data infrastructure, moving from a "custodian-only" model to a distributed, community-driven data lifecycle. Central to this is the ability for human experts and artificial intelligence (AI) agents to enrich Digital Specimens through annotations. However, as AI-driven workflows scale up, there is a risk of specimens becoming annotated with hundreds of low-quality annotations, which threatens synchronization with the source data. Without robust governance, collection managers will face "annotation fatigue," stalling "round-tripping"-the flow of data enrichments back to Collection Management Systems (CMS).

This presentation introduces the DiSSCo Annotation Validation Framework, which went through an international public consultation process in mid-2026. For responsible open digital curation, it treats annotations as first-class digital objects with full provenance, persistent identifiers (Handles) and attribution.

At its technical core, the framework differentiates by the scientific impact of the proposed data change. It aims to find a balance between low-impact corrections, which can be processed efficiently through automated services and high-impact modifications such as taxonomic reidentifications or stratigraphic updates, which should trigger a curated peer-review workflow.

By filtering and prioritizing incoming enrichments, the framework ensures that data round-tripping to source CMS remains high-quality, manageable, and highly trusted. This mechanism effectively closes the loop between external research communities, AI annotators, and physical collection institutions, ensuring Digital Specimens remain dynamic, accurate, and reflective of the latest scientific consensus.

actual.identification_notes: Chair introduced 'Wouter Addink'; content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Wouter Addink, DiSSCo technical director, framed the problem of a curator swamped by thousands of AI annotations that could override records and lose provenance. DiSSCo's planned annotation validation framework runs machine annotation services centrally for all collections and places annotations in layers: an untouched institutional base layer, a community enrichment layer for unvetted annotations, and a curated consensus layer. Annotations pass automated technical validation, then are routed by type and impact: low-impact corrections are auto-promoted, medium-impact ones need a two-agent condition or a trusted agent, and high-impact ones (new identifications, type status, catalogue numbers) need managed expert review. A public consultation was extended to 16 October with an online meeting on 22 October.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: DiSSCo proposes impact-based, layered validation so trusted annotations are promoted automatically and only high-impact ones need expert review.
content_items.why_it_matters: Addresses how to absorb large volumes of human and AI annotations without losing institutional control or provenance, a key prerequisite for AI-assisted curation at scale.
key_points: Scenario: a museum builds an AI annotation service that produces thousands or millions of annotations; directly writing to the CMS loses sovereignty and provenance.
Machine annotation services run in the DiSSCo infrastructure so they can be applied to all participating collections; anyone with ORCID can annotate.
Layers of trust: institutional base layer (untouched), community enrichment layer (unvetted), managed review, and curated consensus layer holding the latest digital specimen version.

Validation flow: submission with persistent identifier and agent ID; automated technical validation (schema, content policies, e.g. no malicious content or exact locations of protected species); automated routing; promotion creating a new version.
All versions are stored, making the system resilient to errors in automated promotion.
Comments and quality flags go to the enrichment layer; delete proposals need administrator review.

Edits are assessed for impact: low (error corrections, measurements) auto-promoted; medium needs two agents agreeing or a trusted agent with a good track record; high (new identification, type status, catalogue number) needs expert review, where experts may also be trusted machines.

Three documents (general concept, technical specifications, governance/policy framework) are under public consultation, extended to 16 October; online meeting 22 October; finalisation by year end, then implementation.

notable_claims.claim: Low-impact annotations like error corrections can be automatically promoted to the consensus layer.
Medium-impact annotations require a two-agent condition or a trusted agent.
The public consultation was extended to 16 October with an online meeting on 22 October.

recommendations: Review the consultation documents, starting with the general concept.
future_work: Finalise the framework documents by end of year and start implementation.

content_items.title: Geonomia: Metadata and Community for Georeferencing

programme.title: Geonomia: Metadata and Community for Georeferencing
programme.session: SYM13A Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
There has been considerable progress and investment into the digitisation of natural history collections, particularly among larger institutions that hold globally distributed specimen collections. These specimen records provide the “what, where, when” evidence used as the basis of much research. Data handling pipelines often include data cleaning steps which enhance our understanding of the core “what, where, when” and other attributes of the specimen record. Attributing these enhancements, along with acknowledging their source, to the digital specimen record is difficult due to the distributed nature of research tasks, many of which take place outside the holding institution of the specimen.

Distributed curation and management of digital specimen records are a necessary step in their use to support specific research interests and objectives, resulting in rich but fragmented, unusable data. Data are easily transferable, though trust in the data is essential for passive cross-institutional collaboration, particularly for subjective and ad-hoc tasks such as georeferencing.

With a focus on improving geographic coordinates or retrospectively adding new spatial data, attendees will be presented with the Geonomia project, which clusters GBIF-mediated specimen data to uncover field collecting patterns. The system includes a georeferencing application which will be demonstrated alongside community workshop outputs focussing on the digital curation of the georeferencing process and outputs. The aim of the project is to encourage the re-integration of comprehensive georeference metadata and continually improve the context of field collecting patterns.

Nicolson, N., Bachman, S. and Whittaker, A. (2026) Geonomia. Available at: https://github.com/geonomia (Accessed: 27/05/2026)

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Nikki Nicholson' (ASR); content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Nicky Nicolson presented Geonomia, a Kew project to make specimens' textual localities computable. Only 13% of Kew's 6.3 million digitised specimens appear on GBIF maps, yet analysis of download predicates behind citations showed two-thirds of users filter spatially, discarding most of Kew's data. Using density-based clustering of collector number and date (collectors move forward in time and space), the team groups specimens into collecting trips across all herbaria's GBIF data, finds outliers, and passes trip-level batches to an LLM to summarise itineraries, habitats and regions, publishing results with Datasette. She argued collecting trips are a useful entity between GBIF's related records and Bionomia's collector careers, and that georeferencing should be shared community work.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Clustering specimens into collecting trips makes georeferencing and AI enrichment more efficient and should be done as a community effort.
content_items.why_it_matters: Tackles the large share of specimen data invisible to spatial queries and offers a reusable approach for batching records meaningfully before applying AI.
key_points: Kew has digitised 6.3 million specimens, but only 13% have coordinates on GBIF; many predate GPS and only have place descriptions.
Analysis of GBIF download predicates for citations of Kew data showed two-thirds used spatial predicates, discarding most Kew data; the same analysis is possible for any GBIF dataset.
Collector number plus date traces a collector's path; density-based clustering finds adjacent collecting events, groups variant locality strings and reveals transcription outliers.
Clusters give context for human georeferencing and tighter context batches for AI.
Used GBIF SQL downloads (vascular plants, species level, one country) to pre-process on GBIF's side, including screening recordedBy values like 'collector unknown'.
Processing ran on a shared HPC facility at the Crop Diversity Institute; LLMs summarised habitats, itineraries (linear traverse vs hub-and-spoke), place names and regions per trip.
Results published as a SQLite database with Datasette; example: a 1964 trip of almost 2,000 specimens with only about a third georeferenced, drawn from many institutions' datasets.
Collecting trips sit between GBIF related-records (event level) and Bionomia careers; hypodigms (specimens cited by taxonomists) are another logical grouping.
methods: density-based clustering on collector number and date

notable_claims.claim: Only 13% of Kew's data appear on the GBIF map.
Two-thirds of downloads citing Kew data used spatial predicates.
Collectors can only move forward through time, so collector number against date traces their activity.

recommendations: Treat georeferencing and automated enrichment as shared community tasks.
Do not treat specimens as atomic units for AI; batch them meaningfully.
results_findings: An example 1964 trip of almost 2,000 specimens with only about a third georeferenced, contributed by many datasets.

content_items.title: From satellite embeddings to Darwin Core: an open, ensemble-AI workflow for Prosopis juliflora mapping and reusable training-dataset generation

programme.title: From satellite embeddings to Darwin Core: an open, ensemble-AI workflow for Prosopis juliflora mapping and reusable training-dataset generation
programme.session: SYM13A Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Prosopis juliflora is among the most consequential invaders of global drylands, drawing down groundwater, depressing crop yields, and displacing grassland and pastoral commons. In Kutch, Gujarat, where Prosopis has overrun gauchar lands and Banni grassland fringes, classifier outputs guide biomass sourcing for a pyrolysis facility at Anjar, so every update carries operational consequence.

The pipeline fuses three openly licensed inputs on Google Earth Engine. AlphaEarth embeddings provide a learned per-pixel representation. Sentinel-2 contributes NDVI and EVI. SRTM derivatives (slope, roughness, TPI) separate Prosopis from similar canopy on rocky slopes. A four-model ensemble (two Random Forests, GTB, CART) is trained on versioned polygons tagged by source: presences, absences, false-positive corrections, and positive refinements. The correction loop turns model errors into named, attributable training records rather than silently retraining over them. Ensemble accuracy reaches ~91% on held-out test data.

Layered masks (hills, water, road buffers) exclude implausible pixels; each is a named, recorded operation with justification and source, auditable downstream.

Every positive pixel becomes a Darwin Core occurrence with basisOfRecord=MachineObservation, coordinateUncertaintyInMeters from pixel geometry, and identifiedBy naming both human curators and model version. Ensemble probability is carried as a MeasurementOrFact extension. The dataset, training polygons (CC BY 4.0), mask metadata, and model artefact are structured for GBIF publication, closing the round-trip from human curation to AI enrichment to reusable training material.

actual.identification_notes: Self-introduced as Pranav Jha; organisation name as transcribed ('Climatra Carbon') may be an ASR rendering. The talk did not explicitly describe the Darwin Core output promised in the title.

content_items.summary: Pranav Jha described mapping the invasive Prosopis juliflora (Neltuma juliflora) across India, especially about 1.1 million hectares in Kutch, Gujarat, using satellite data and geospatial foundation model embeddings. The workflow combines Sentinel, hyperspectral and NISAR radar data with ground truthing, AlphaEarth embeddings, NDVI and slope checks, reaching about 91% accuracy, and uses 3 m hyperspectral signatures to distinguish Prosopis from similar natives. Ground teams validate predicted clusters through drop, curation and refined zones to build reusable training datasets, and the model is being extended to Lantana camara and mangroves.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Satellite embeddings plus hyperspectral signatures and ground validation can map invasive Prosopis at scale and generate reusable, attributable training data.
content_items.why_it_matters: Links remote sensing AI to biodiversity data reuse, with a focus on transparent, reusable evidence for invasive species management.
key_points: Prosopis juliflora is among IUCN's top invasive species and has spread across APAC and sub-Saharan Africa; in Kutch it covers about 1.1 million hectares, harming native species and pastoral communities, and has spread to 20+ agroclimatic zones.
Satellite mapping is needed to understand invasion at scale, over time (multi-date imagery), where to look next and what it displaces.
Density is mapped at 10 m resolution to guide ground teams to hotspots.

Inputs: Sentinel, hyperspectral (e.g. AVIRIS and others), NISAR SAR data and ground truth; AlphaEarth geospatial foundation model embeddings train a classifier, followed by NDVI and slope/elevation checks.
Current accuracy about 91%; working with Google DeepMind to include it in Google Earth.
Prosopis resembles native Prosopis cineraria and acacias; 3 m hyperspectral spectroscopy separates them.
Ground workflow of drop, curating and refined zones produces reusable datasets; goal is transparent, attributable, reusable evidence.
Next: Lantana camara in northern India and mangroves in sub-Saharan regions.

notable_claims.claim: Prosopis juliflora covers about 1.1 million hectares of Kutch, Gujarat.
The current model accuracy is 91%.

limitations: Prosopis is spectrally and visually similar to native species and can be confused by ground teams.
future_work: Extend to Lantana camara and mangroves.

Distinguishing Prosopis from look-alike natives with hyperspectral data.

content_items.title: Open Digital Curation and Round-Tripping Biodiversity Data Enhancements Across Collection Infrastructures: Six Years and 50 Million Links in Bionomia

programme.title: Open Digital Curation and Round-Tripping Biodiversity Data Enhancements Across Collection Infrastructures: Six Years and 50 Million Links in Bionomia
programme.session: SYM13B Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Throughout the past 6 years, [Bionomia](https://bionomia.net) has supported open digital curation through machine-readable annotations, bidirectional synchronization workflows, and contributor attribution that preserves curatorial authority while enabling broader participation. Case studies will illustrate how annotations involving specimen linkages can be generated by humans and redistributed back to source repositories rather than remaining isolated within downstream aggregators. Bionomia’s data processing tools, services, and outputs enable lightweight integration with collection management systems while preserving institutional ownership and editorial control over incoming enhancements. Recently, the human name parsing tool was successfully ported to a high-performance Go package using Claude AI. The platform also exposes mechanisms for crediting contributors in ways that support professional recognition, reproducibility, and reuse. The continuous cycle of incremental enhancements has not been without its technical challenges, and these will be discussed in relation to Darwin Core and data exchange structures used by our community. By framing digital curation as an ongoing and collaborative process rather than a terminal publication event, Bionomia demonstrates how round-tripping infrastructures can strengthen resilience, trust, outreach, and long-term stewardship across biodiversity data ecosystems despite uncertainties about any one project's governance and sustainability.

actual.identification_notes: Virtual pre-recorded talk; the chair welcomed David Shorthouse, and the video initially played only as audio before being fixed.

content_items.summary: In a pre-recorded talk, David Shorthouse questioned calls for taxonomists to train AI identification models without credit, and highlighted that 60% of preserved specimens in GBIF lack any identifiedBy value. He reviewed six years of Bionomia: services for individuals (alerts when specimens are used in research, Zenodo archives with DOIs) and for organisations (frictionless data packages of CSV files, badges), and the potential of the collector social network for attribution suggestions. He identified unstable occurrence identifiers as the main barrier to round-tripping, noted no CMS can record third-party attribution provenance, and discussed the Darwin Core Data Package's agent terms, predicting recordedByID and identifiedByID will become obsolete and calling for a TDWG task group on an agent role vocabulary.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Round-tripping is much harder than expected, and data managers must fully populate identifiedBy so taxonomists' expertise is credited.
content_items.why_it_matters: A reflective, data-backed critique of how collections credit expertise and how AI and round-tripping can erode or build trust.
key_points: A 2025 paper trained a herbarium-image identifier to 90% accuracy and recommended taxonomists train models, which he framed as working oneself out of a career without credit.
About 60% of preserved specimens published to GBIF have no identifiedBy content, undermining efforts like the EU TETTRIs project.
Bionomia is in its sixth year; anyone with ORCID can link specimens to collectors and determiners; interface in seven languages; ~320 million records re-downloaded monthly from GBIF.

DwC-DP will let over-prescribed terms (recordedBy, identifiedBy) be expressed as agent-role-action relationships; he predicts recordedByID and identifiedByID will be deprecated, questions the 'preferred' prefix in agent name, and calls for a TDWG Attribution Interest Group task group to ratify agent roles (perhaps modelled on the OBO Contributor Role Ontology).
The co-collector social network can boost candidate matches and could support a lightweight attribution utility within a CMS.

User services: email alerts when one's specimens are used in research; Zenodo snapshots with DOIs for CVs. Organisation services: frictionless data package of CSVs (users, missing attributions, date conflicts) and HTML badges.
Main barrier: unstable occurrence identifiers from dataset deletions, splits and migrations; catalogue number is often the more stable key.
No organisation can absorb full provenance of volunteer-made links; DwC-DP's provenance table may get close.
themes_raw: agent roles in Darwin Core Data Package
methods: frictionless CSV data packages for round-tripping

notable_claims.claim: A full 60% of preserved specimens published by museums and herbaria in GBIF have no content in identifiedBy.
Roughly 320 million occurrence records are re-downloaded from GBIF into Bionomia each month.
The single greatest problem for round-tripping is unstable identifiers for occurrences.
No organisation has shown readiness to absorb the full provenance of attribution links created by Bionomia volunteers.

recommendations: Fully populate identifiedBy or its DwC-DP equivalent.
Form a TDWG task group to ratify an agent role vocabulary.
Build services that deliver value to individual users to drive uptake.
limitations: Bionomia cannot yet accept attributions on extension rows such as identification history, nor record volunteers' evidence for links.

representative_excerpt.text: The role of the specialist taxonomist should be to do good taxonomy. The role of the data manager is to not omit metadata that is essential for taxonomists and others to illustrate their expertise.
