content_items.title: Type specimens in Wikidata

programme.title: Type specimens in Wikidata
programme.session: SYM13B Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Type specimens play a vital role in ensuring the correct application of scientific names. Recently a type specimen data model has been created for Wikidata. This data model results from work undertaken by participants of the [Wikidata:WikiProject Natural History Specimen Data Mode](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:WikiProject_Natural_History_Specimen_Data_Model)l. The data model encourages the creation of type specimen Wikidata items that link to appropriately structured data. Several Wikidata properties were proposed and accepted by the Wikidata community to facilitate the formation of this data model. The data model also encourages the linking of institutional identifiers to appropriate type specimen items.

Documentation was produced to guide editors in the creation and linking of type specimen Wikidata items. This included an exemplar spreadsheet generated from an OpenRefine project creating Wikidata items for holotype specimens held in the New Zealand Arthropod Collection.

A data model for structured data on Wikimedian Commons was also proposed by the WikiProject. This is intended to apply to natural history specimen media files added to Wikimedia Commons. Again documentation was produced to assist editors to create or add appropriate structured data to natural history specimen image files.

One of the core aims of the WikiProject was to align specimen and type-material modelling across Wikimedia projects with existing biodiversity informatics standards. As a result crosswalk documentation was produced to illustrate the mapping between fields of the Wikidata type specimen data model and Darwin Core. Crosswalk documentation was also produced mapping Wikidata properties used to add structured data on Wikimedia Commons to media files and equivalent Darwin Core terms.

actual.identification_notes: Slides could not be displayed in the room (technical difficulties 05:45:14-05:47:16); she gave the talk without them and pointed to slides on Zenodo.

content_items.summary: Siobhan Leachman presented a proposed Wikidata data model for type specimens, developed with Auckland Museum, Te Papa, the Bioeconomy Science Institute and Wikidata editors to fix inconsistent modelling. Wikidata is intended as a non-canonical finding aid bridging sources and identifiers, with references and edit history supporting transparent reuse by AI applications. The model was built from existing items, likely queries and a crosswalk to Darwin Core; new properties (collector, specimen classifier, collection date, location collected) were proposed, and a trial batch of New Zealand Arthropod Collection holotypes was uploaded via OpenRefine from GBIF data. Documentation is on a WikiProject, Wikimedia Commons and a Zenodo community; future work includes GBIF occurrence ID, basis of record, preservation method and biocultural notice properties.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A consistent Wikidata type specimen model lets anyone link type specimens to collectors, publications, taxa and identifiers as a transparent finding aid.
content_items.why_it_matters: Improves findability and interoperability of type specimens and gives AI applications a well-referenced, provenance-rich source.
key_points: Motivation: inconsistent modelling of existing type specimen items; helping institutions translate Darwin Core data into Wikidata; supporting the digital extended specimen.
Wikidata tracks references per statement and all edits, supporting transparency and provenance for AI reuse.
Wikidata data are not canonical; they are a finding aid linking to the holding institution's data.
Approach: compare existing items, review standards including Darwin Core, design for likely queries, be pragmatic for institutions already publishing to GBIF.
New properties proposed for collector, specimen classifier, collection date and location collected.
Trial batch: holotypes of the New Zealand Arthropod Collection extracted from GBIF, cleaned and reconciled in OpenRefine, uploaded to Wikidata.
Documentation on a WikiProject, Wikimedia Commons and Zenodo (including the OpenRefine spreadsheet); exemplar items include a holotype first observed on iNaturalist and one linked to a DiSSCo DOI.
Future: GBIF occurrence ID property (under discussion), basis of record property, preservation method, and biocultural/Local Contexts notices once GBIF and Darwin Core support exists.

notable_claims.claim: Data added under the model is not intended to be canonical; Wikidata is a finding aid.
New properties were proposed for collector, specimen classifier, collection date and location collected.

future_work: Propose properties for GBIF occurrence ID, basis of record, preservation method and biocultural notices.
examples_case_studies: Exemplar holotype items linking iNaturalist observations and DiSSCo DOIs.

notable_moments.description: Wikidata as a transparent source for responsible AI.
Trial upload of NZ Arthropod Collection holotypes.
Known gaps and future property proposals.

content_items.title: Here, There, and Everywhere: Modelling Research Expeditions in Wikidata

programme.title: Here, There, and Everywhere: Modelling Research Expeditions in Wikidata
programme.session: SYM13B Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Research expeditions are major sources of natural history collections and connect distributed cultural heritage across institutions and countries. However, expedition data remain fragmented, inconsistently modelled, and often lack stable identifiers. This hampers discoverability, interoperability, and provenance tracking, while also limiting efforts to contextualise collecting events and practices within their broader historical context. The TDWG Task Group “Modelling Research Expeditions” developed recommendations for modelling and linking of expedition data, working towards a shared terminology, a reusable data model and schema, and best practices for publishing expedition metadata as Linked Open Data.

The presentation proposes recommendations for an expedition data model connecting both historical and contemporary collecting events with specimens and other objects, participants, institutions, localities, itineraries, publications, and archival records. Particular emphasis is placed on interoperability with Darwin Core, the use of Wikidata identifiers, and collaborative community curation of expedition metadata as a complement or even replacement for the round-tripping of data back into collection databases. The recommendations aim to improve data quality, facilitate cross-institutional linking, annotation and validation workflows, and transparency regarding the historical context of collecting activities. By enabling machine-readable and multilingual representation of expedition data, the proposed model contributes to making collection data more FAIR and supports broader reuse in e.g., knowledge graphs, visualisation tools, and digital humanities research.

actual.identification_notes: Self-introduced as 'Sabine von Mehring' (ASR) of Museum für Naturkunde; spoke for the task group. Room display issues continued but the PDF slides worked.

content_items.summary: Sabine von Mering presented on behalf of the TDWG Research Expeditions task group (Collection Descriptions Interest Group). Expedition data are fragmented across institutions and lack persistent identifiers, hindering provenance and historical, including colonial, contextualisation. The group has a draft definition of a research expedition, promotes Wikidata QIDs as identifiers for expedition parent events, and proposes a lightweight, extensible Wikidata schema with minimum properties, links to holding collections and archives, and knowledge-graph visualisation (e.g. Scholia for the Harriman Alaska Expedition). Recommendations: create or enrich expedition items, use minimum properties, and record QIDs in collection management systems.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Treat research expeditions as first-class entities with Wikidata identifiers so distributed specimens, people, publications and archives can be linked.
content_items.why_it_matters: Improves discoverability and provenance of expedition-derived collections and supports historical and colonial-context research.
key_points: Expeditions were often transdisciplinary, so specimens, ethnographic objects and archives are scattered across institutions.
The terms research/scientific expedition are not unproblematic given colonial, economic and military entanglements.

Working definition: an organised, time-bounded field activity by one or more people at one or more locations, affiliated with an institution, for research purposes, distinct from routine collecting (still a draft).
In GBIF an expedition can be an event, linked via parentEventID; some datasets already use Wikidata QIDs; longer-term explicit Darwin Core support is being considered alongside DwC-DP.
Minimum recommended Wikidata properties: instance of, start/end time, country, participants, collection items at, archives at; extensible with funder, field of work, itinerary etc.
Links to holding collections can reference specimen PIDs; archival material (logbooks, field books, correspondence) and finding aids are recorded.
Scholia knowledge graph of the Harriman Alaska Expedition shows participants, publications and collections.
Recommendations will be finalised and published; institutions are encouraged to contribute, including hidden contributors visible only in archives.

notable_claims.claim: Expedition data remain fragmented, inconsistently modelled and often lack persistent identifiers.
In GBIF an expedition can already be represented as an event linked through parentEventID.

recommendations: Create or enrich Wikidata items for research expeditions where you hold institutional knowledge and archives.
Use the minimum recommended properties and extend as appropriate.
Record expedition QIDs in collection management systems.
future_work: Finalise and publish the recommendations; consider explicit expedition support in Darwin Core.
examples_case_studies: Harriman Alaska Expedition Wikidata item and Scholia graph.

notable_moments.description: Working definition of a research expedition.
Harriman Alaska Expedition item.
Recommendations to institutions.

content_items.title: Digital curation across the biodiversity data lifecycle, at the node level (SiB Colombia), aggregator level (GBIF) and how to incorporate user feedback

programme.title: Digital curation across the biodiversity data lifecycle, at the node level (SiB Colombia), aggregator level (GBIF) and how to incorporate user feedback
programme.session: SYM13B Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Digital curation should be a continuous process through the biodiversity data lifecycle. Within the GBIF ecosystem, it starts at the publishing level facilitated by GBIF nodes, continues with quality checks done automatically by GBIF Data Processing and incorporates user feedback provided through GBIF.org or when publishers are contacted directly.

Here we will explain how the data curation is done at SiB Colombia as one example of a GBIF node. Using a publishing support model called “acompañamientos”, where a dedicated helpdesk team reviews some prioritized DwC elements and provides feedback to publishers before publication. With the main goal of facilitating data mobilization by ensuring the data is as complete as possible, meets quality requirements and is free of consistency errors.

The next step is the data processing done automatically by GBIF pipelines before ingestion, addressing some of the most common and relevant elements for users, such as dates, coordinates, controlled vocabularies, etc. These quality flags allow publishers and users to review and improve their data.

The next section covers how the user feedback is currently handled on GBIF, for taxonomic issues that are handled with a human/AI approach, where an AI agent generates JSON tags that are later reviewed by a human team that ensures results are correct and there are no hallucinations.

We also present an overview of user feedback related to occurrence records, covering how much feedback arrives at GBIF, how often publishers respond, and whether they are willing to correct their data.

Finally, we will explore how things can be improved on all fronts to have better data curation and round tripping in the long run for GBIF mediated data.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by first name (Esteban); formerly at SiB Colombia; includes short Q&A with the chair.

content_items.summary: Esteban Marentes described curation as a circular process with feedback loops at node, aggregator and user levels. At SiB Colombia, every dataset receives human 'acompañamiento' - a semi-automatic review with OpenRefine, the GBIF API and QGIS of metadata and 30-40 Darwin Core elements - before publication. GBIF interprets names and other fields and exposes flags through the Data Validator and annotated downloads. Of about 700 helpdesk messages in three months, 45% of taxonomy issues and about 37% of data-content issues were fixed; an LLM in GitHub Actions summarises taxonomic feedback into JSON (edited by staff about 70% of the time) and a deterministic script checks the Catalogue of Life extended release to close resolved issues.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Curation feedback works at every stage of the data lifecycle, and about a third or more of reported issues do get fixed; AI is used cautiously to summarise feedback.
content_items.why_it_matters: Quantifies how user feedback flows back to data and shows a careful, human-reviewed use of LLMs in aggregator operations.
key_points: Data flow: publisher -> node/data manager feedback -> GBIF feedback -> users providing feedback to GBIF, nodes or publishers; nodes differ in approach.
SiB Colombia reviews every dataset before GBIF publication using OpenRefine, the GBIF API and QGIS, recording fixes and required changes in an Excel report; publication only after fixes.
GBIF interprets names, elevations, dates and vocabularies and raises flags (fuzzy taxon match, invalid date, invalid coordinates).
Publishers can use the GBIF Data Validator; users can see issues in annotated downloads and dataset-level summaries.
Roughly 700 helpdesk messages in Q1: mostly general help, then IPT, then taxonomy; 46 about data content.
About 45% of taxonomy feedback fixed, largely via the Catalogue of Life extended release; about 37% of data content issues fixed by publishers.

An OpenAI LLM in GitHub Actions summarises taxonomic feedback into categorised JSON; staff edit about 70% of outputs; a deterministic script re-checks each issue against the latest CoL extended release monthly.
Q&A: no community feedback yet on the AI use; SiB Colombia is exploring AI to speed up reviews; models improve quickly.
methods: LLM summarisation into JSON with human review

notable_claims.claim: GBIF's helpdesk received roughly 700 messages in the first three months of the year.
About 45% of taxonomy feedback had been fixed, thanks to the Catalogue of Life extended release.
Staff update the LLM-generated JSON about 70% of the time.

results_findings: About 37% of data-content feedback issues were fixed by publishers.

q_and_a.question: Do you get feedback from your community on the use of AI?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Not yet; it is new and only summarises feedback to save time; SiB Colombia is starting to explore AI for reviews.

notable_moments.description: SiB Colombia's pre-publication acompañamiento.
How much feedback actually gets fixed.
LLM plus deterministic checks for taxonomic feedback.

content_items.title: Closing Gaps in Specimen Metadata: A Collaborative Annotation and Feedback Platform for Natural History Collections

programme.title: Closing Gaps in Specimen Metadata: A Collaborative Annotation and Feedback Platform for Natural History Collections
programme.session: SYM13B Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
While the digitization of natural history collections is accelerating globally, GBIF data trends reveal a critical bottleneck: a persistent gap in the completeness of digitized specimen records. Many records still lack essential metadata, specifically accurate taxonomic classifications, precise geospatial coordinates, and explicit collection dates. Bridging these gaps requires a systematic, scalable annotation mechanism.

Inspired by collaborative frameworks such as the European DiSSCover initiative, we developed an annotation platform tailored for digital specimens. The platform ingests natural history collection data from the Taiwan Biodiversity Information Alliance (TBIA). The platform allows users to query target specimens by data completeness or holding institution through filtering functions. To optimize the workflow, it pairs an intuitive manual interface with AI-assisted data extraction, enabling users to verify and adjust AI-generated transcriptions to increase processing efficiency.

Aggregated annotations form a trackable feedback loop, allowing enriched records to be returned to the original data providers for review and merging into their primary databases. This continuous cycle improves the quality of open data while lowering the barrier to participation for smaller institutions. Collections from institutions without sufficient staff often fail to transcribe labels fast enough to keep pace with imaging; the platform lets them publish specimen images early and recruit public contributors to fill in the data, increasing the usability of their holdings and encouraging institutions with un-digitized collections to join the biodiversity informatics community.

speakers.name: Szu-Hsien Lee
speakers.affiliation: Biodiversity Research Museum, Academia Sinica, Taiwan

actual.identification_notes: Self-introduced as 'Shih-Hsen Li' (ASR); chair also renders the name variously. Content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Szu-Hsien Lee showed GBIF data trends indicating that specimen records increasingly lag observation records in completeness, because imaging is fast but transcription needs experts (including for Western and Japanese-era labels in Taiwan). After using students and AI within one institution, he built a system over the Taiwan Biodiversity Information Alliance (TBIA) aggregate (about 2 million specimen records) where anyone can fill missing terms with AI-assisted transcription and human correction, storing both for later evaluation. He also demonstrated collector trip views and links to historical botanical literature, and aims to return corrections to providers, arguing 'an untranscribed image is not a failure, it's an invitation'.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A national collaborative annotation platform with AI-assisted transcription can close metadata gaps across many Taiwanese collections.
content_items.why_it_matters: Addresses the widening completeness gap of specimen data and offers a model for institutions lacking digitisation resources.
key_points: GBIF data trends show specimen records growing but lacking completeness (dates, identifications, coordinates), with the gap widening globally and in Taiwan.
Imaging takes seconds; transcription of old handwriting (including Japanese-era labels) needs trained experts and funding.
The museum's collection management system is shared with other Taiwanese institutions lacking resources; images without metadata are effectively hidden.
College teachers assigned transcription as student homework; later AI was used, but this only helped one institution slowly.
TBIA aggregates biodiversity data from institutions and government in Taiwan (also published to GBIF); about 2 million natural history specimen records.

Flags: about 30% missing identification (often name-matching issues, resolved via the TaiCOL checklist), over 65% missing coordinates (often with verbatim locality), and missing media is the biggest barrier.
Platform integrates an AI API for transcription; AI handles English handwriting well but struggles with Chinese and Japanese, so humans correct; both versions are stored for later evaluation.
Future: route accepted corrections back to data providers and encourage undigitised institutions; sync collector names with Bionomia and Wikidata.

Over 65% of TBIA specimen records lack coordinates, though most have verbatim locality.

limitations: AI transcription is weak for Chinese and Japanese handwriting.
Records without images cannot be transcribed.
future_work: Return corrected data to providers for republication.
Sync collector names with Bionomia and Wikidata.

The annotation platform interface.

content_items.title: Responsible and GreenAI: Does our community need Gigantic Data Centers to deliver?

programme.title: Responsible and GreenAI: Does our community need Gigantic Data Centers to deliver?
programme.session: SYM13B Responsible AI, Open Digital Curation, and Round-Tripping for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Both the public and private sectors invest billions in AI. Key players notably in the US, China and the EU try to outcompete each other by releasing the fastest and most powerful Large Language Models (LLMs) and building the largest data centers to cope with the increasing demand for computational power. AI Factories are end-to-end systems that continuously turn data into AI models and AI-powered services at scale. For example, in February 2025, the EU launched the InvestAI initiative to mobilise €200 billion in broader AI investment, including a dedicated €20 billion European fund for AI Gigafactories. In the US, figures around 500 billion US$ invested in AI infrastructures are cited, with similar figures being estimated from China. Looking at the global scale, with the digitisation efforts and open science policies, billions of data points and media resources around biodiversity are made available and potential candidates for AI applications. One may argue that our discipline is actually in need of such large resources to deliver. When sizing down to specific taxon levels or smaller geographic areas, training datasets of several 100 000 to less than 1 Mio of records managed to deliver accurate AI models for automated species recognition based on images or sounds. programme.title: Agentic AI Systems for Specimen Interaction and Camera-Based Observation
programme.session: LT17 Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
programme.abstract: The study, recording and interpretation of natural history specimens is a highly contextual activity, drawing on curatorial expertise, published literature, collections data and comparative knowledge across taxa. In many cases, working with specimens is also a physical process, requiring observation, annotation, transcription, imaging and careful handling. These activities are time-consuming and can limit the number of specimens that can be examined, recorded or reinterpreted at scale. This presentation explores the development of an agentic AI system capable of interacting with physical specimens through a dedicated imaging and specimen observation platform. Operating on local/on-device hardware, the system integrates large language models, computer vision, camera control and hardware control to support direct observation and interpretation of specimens within collections environments. The system uses a camera-based platform to capture visual data from specimens and incorporate this information into the model’s reasoning process. By combining visual input with collections data and relevant literature, the agent can support tasks such as specimen inspection, metadata verification, annotation and morphological interpretation. Through the integration of RAG, the system links observed specimens to contextual knowledge, enabling more informed and interactive analysis. This establishes a foundation for embodied AI within museum settings, where models can move beyond static datasets and engage more directly with physical collections. Live demonstrations will show how such systems can support curatorial and research workflows, providing a new interface between researchers, AI systems and physical specimens while maintaining local control over data, models and processing.

content_items.title: Rediscovering Archives - Using LLM's for the Transcription and Extraction of Ecological Data from Historical Archives

programme.title: Rediscovering Archives - Using LLM’s for the Transcription and Extraction of Ecological Data from Historical Archives
programme.session: LT17 Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
programme.abstract:
Historical archives held by museums and research institutions contain vast quantities of material that remain underutilised due to limitations in accessibility, readability, and searchability. Recent advances in multimodal large language models (LLMs) present new opportunities for improving access to these collections, particularly for complex historical documents that challenge conventional optical character recognition (OCR) and handwritten text recognition (HTR) approaches. This is especially relevant within natural history archives, where materials range from structured to unstructured, often containing handwritten and typed text alongside historical terminology.

This project investigates the use of multimodal LLMs for the transcription and interpretation of historical archival documents, with a focus on prompt engineering and schema-guided extraction to produce structured, machine-readable outputs. We focus on natural history collection materials such as those housed at Natural History Museum, UK, and Zoological Society London, as well as publicly available datasets such as the India Office botanical records from the British Library. Our study evaluates transcription performance - measured by Levenshtein distance, word error rate, and character error rate - across mixed-format, handwritten documents against ground truth transcriptions. By examining how multimodal LLMs perform on ecologically and historically relevant archival materials, this work contributes to emerging research on AI-assisted archival accessibility and explores how historical collections can be transformed into structured digital resources suitable for biodiversity and historical research.

programme.abstract: The continuous monitoring of the Common Gull (Larus canus) breeding colony on Kakrarahu islet in the Baltic Sea, Estonia, is one of the region's longest-running ecological research projects, dating back to 1962. With continuous breeding success data collected since 1968 and ringing and age data since 1971, this project holds a vast repository of longitudinal population dynamics data. Historically, these data were recorded in field notebooks, systematized on catalogue cards, and later partially transferred to spreadsheets. Modern data collection has now transitioned to a specialized mobile application for real-time field use. This work-in-progress project outlines the ongoing effort to rescue and digitize this extensive legacy dataset using a hybrid approach of manual data entry and novel AI-based digitization techniques and store it together with the latest field data. Because the monitoring methodology has remained constant over the decades, the recovered data holds immense value for understanding long-term population dynamics. The primary goal of this initiative is to make these unique ecological data widely available following FAIR principles. While multiple open-access publication approaches will ultimately be utilized, this presentation focuses on one particular pathway. By utilizing PlutoF, a comprehensive common data space for biodiversity developed by the University of Tartu, we establish a pipeline to structure, store, and publish the historical dataset to the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF). This workflow demonstrates an effective framework for rescuing legacy mass-monitoring data and ensuring over six decades of ecological observations become globally accessible.

programme.abstract:
Sustainable finance increasingly demands biodiversity data and metrics, yet these are only credible when underlying data are traceable, quality-assessed, and explicit about uncertainty. Currently, the financial sector faces a "biodiversity data gap": existing datasets are sparse and taxonomically biased, and often lack the depth needed for reliable risk assessments. Without robust data standards, investors cannot reliably evaluate the local impact of their portfolios or meet emerging nature-positive targets.

Drawing on insights from the Mistra FinBio program, we identify critical roadblocks in biodiversity reporting and propose a key improvement: a "data quality hierarchy." By mapping data and model outcomes to quality tiers and standardized metadata, it would enable AI-ready data for financial risk models, turning observations into trustworthy, decision-ready inputs.

The TDWG community is invited to collaborate on closing this data gap, focusing on improving data quality standards. Biodiversity data should not just be collected, but made interoperable, machine-actionable, and ready for the next generation of sustainability reporting.

content_items.title: Robots Rapidly Writing Records: Machine Annotations at Scale with DiSSCo

programme.title: Robots Rapidly Writing Records: Machine Annotations at Scale with DiSSCo
programme.session: LT17 Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
programme.abstract:
In the face of the biodiversity crisis, digitization efforts in natural science collections need to rapidly increase. Scaling up these efforts requires the support of the community - and machines. DiSSCo, the Distributed System of Scientific Collections, enables this through annotation and harmonization of the data.

When natural science collection datasets are ingested into DiSSCo, specimens are transformed into Digital Specimens, assigned a Persistent Identifier, harmonized to a shared data model, and become and become fully actionable by machines as discrete knowledge units.

Through this process, DiSSCo enables community curation through annotations by humans and machines. With Digital Specimens harmonized to one data model across host institutions, DiSSCo is uniquely situated to host “plug and play” machine services to act on any specimen in the DiSSCo infrastructure. Instead of being confined to a single dataset they were designed for, Machine Annotation Services (MAS) adapted for DiSSCo can act on any Digital Specimen, breaking institutional silos and furthering collaboration.

For the first time, DiSSCo MASs have been tested at scale, running on all digital objects in a dataset as they are ingested into the DiSSCo infrastructure. These pilot services link all Digital Specimens in a given dataset to counterparts that can be found in GBIF, ENA, or BOLD. With the pilot successful, there is now an opportunity to run more complex services (such as label transcription using large language models) at scale on natural science collection data in DiSSCo.

This lightning talk gives an overview of the MAS-on-Ingestion feature in DiSSCo and what that means for transforming collection data.

programme.abstract:
Over 724 million entomological specimens exist worldwide. The collection at the Norwegian Institute of Bioeconomy Research (NIBIO) holds approximately 200,000 partly databased specimens, highlighting the urgent need for digitisation with high-quality images and structured metadata to support research and outreach.

We asked: what can be built in one week to initiate digitising a small collection, and how can AI enhance the process?

During a joint visit between NIBIO (Division of Biotechnology and Plant Health) and the Natural History Museum UK (AI & Innovation), we developed a functional, low-cost imaging setup using recycled office materials, simple LED lighting, and two borrowed cameras (Nikon Z7 and Z7 II). The aim was not perfection, but speed, accessibility, and replicability. We focused on Scolytinae (bark beetles), a group central to NIBIO’s research. Specimens of varying sizes were imaged in dorsal and lateral views and filmed in 360° rotation. In total, several hundred specimens were captured, producing a compact but versatile dataset. This dataset was used in three AI pipelines: (1) CNNs trained for species classification; (2) 3D reconstruction from video to generate interactive models for outreach; and (3) combined CNN and LLM approaches to extract specimen label data directly from videos. Together, these experiments demonstrate that rapid, low-cost digitisation can meaningfully support AI-driven classification, data extraction, and engagement, providing a scalable entry point for modernising biological collections.

As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into biodiversity data infrastructures, AI-generated annotations, classifications, and metadata are reshaping how biodiversity knowledge is organized, interpreted, and governed. While large language models and other generative AI systems create new opportunities for metadata enrichment, semantic integration, and data discovery, they also introduce challenges related to interpretability, semantic consistency, provenance, and institutional trust. This presentation examines biodiversity infrastructures from a knowledge organization perspective, focusing on how probabilistic AI outputs interact with structured biodiversity standards, controlled vocabularies, and long-standing cataloguing practices. The talk will explore emerging challenges surrounding semantic ambiguity, machine-generated biodiversity knowledge, and the governance of AI-assisted curation workflows within biodiversity repositories. Particular attention will be given to the need for provenance-aware, semantically transparent, and interoperable approaches that align AI-generated outputs with community standards and reproducible biodiversity data practices. content_items.title: kabr-tools: A Modular Workflow for Automated Video-Based Behavioral Monitoring Across the Autonomy Spectrum

programme.title: kabr-tools: A Modular Workflow for Automated Video-Based Behavioral Monitoring Across the Autonomy Spectrum
programme.session: LT17 Bots, Bits, and Biodiversity
programme.abstract: Quantifying animal behavior from video footage is central to conservation and welfare assessment, but drone and camera-trap deployments now generate datasets that are too large to process manually. Existing tools support individual stages of video-to-behavior processing, yet ecologists lack practical guidance on which stages can be reliably automated and which require manual review. We present kabr-tools, an open-source modular workflow for video-based behavioral monitoring that supports a spectrum of autonomy, from fully manual annotation to fully automated processing. Components for detection, tracking, and classification are interchangeable and taxon-agnostic, producing structured outputs that align with biodiversity data standards. We evaluate the workflow against expert annotation at each pipeline stage and trace how errors propagate into downstream behavioral estimates, using drone footage of Grevy's zebras, Plains zebras, and reticulated giraffes at Mpala Research Centre, Kenya, and drone and camera trap footage of African wild dogs at The Wilds, Ohio. Detection is the primary bottleneck in both systems, since once individuals were reliably detected, tracking and classification added limited additional error for common behaviors. Automated classification achieved 91.3-F1 for the three most frequent ungulate behaviors, declining to 50.3-F1 for rare categories. A camera-source ablation confirmed that tail-class failure reflects insufficient training examples rather than a modality-specific limitation. This error characterization positions animal behavior studies on the autonomy spectrum, given their research question and required precision, and highlights where standardized, machine-actionable behavioral outputs depend on targeted human review.

The modular workflow runs from drone or camera-trap video collection through model-agnostic detection, tracking and behaviour annotation with manual oversight, to ecological analyses such as time budgets, behaviour transitions and individual behaviour patterns, and has been used for African wild dog studies.

content_items.summary: After the lightning talks the moderators opened questions. Besides questions to individual speakers (captured with those talks), an audience member asked whether speakers found hallucinations when reviewing AI outputs. The answer (apparently from a collaborator of Jenna Kline) was that non-generative ML tools don't hallucinate but misclassify, and accuracy should be evaluated at the ecological task level because of distribution shift; Jack Hollister acknowledged validating vast LLM outputs is an unsolved problem; a relayed comment argued ML behaviour annotation beats humans. The session closed with feedback that Q&A in lightning sessions needs better support.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Validation of large-scale AI output remains open; for ML classifiers, accuracy should be judged on the ecological task rather than benchmark metrics.
content_items.why_it_matters: Highlights evaluation practices for AI in biodiversity and practical lessons for running lightning sessions.
key_points: Question to all: have you found hallucinations, and does not finding any mean none exist or they were undetected?

Answer: non-generative ML has no hallucinations but has expected misclassifications; evaluate accuracy at the ecological task level because ML accuracy is misleading once deployed under distribution shift.
Jack Hollister: LLM outputs are too large to validate fully; how to find small hallucinations is an open question.
Relayed from Jenna Kline: ML-based behaviour classification can be better than human analysis; latent-space approaches (Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior) address unnamed behaviours.
Audience feedback: the one-minute format and app made asking questions hard; moderators suggested better aids listing talks at the end.
